title: Chapter 2 Drill: Ethics, Evidence, Patient Safety, and Women's Health Systems

items.stem: Researchers want to learn whether a rare congenital anomaly is associated with first-trimester use of a medication. Which study design is most efficient for this rare outcome?
options: Randomized controlled trial
Cross-sectional survey
Case-control study
Prospective cohort study
items.explanation: A case-control study starts with people who have the outcome and a comparison group without it, then looks back at exposure, which makes it efficient for rare outcomes and yields an odds ratio. A randomized trial of a possible teratogen would be unethical and underpowered for a rare event. A prospective cohort would need enormous numbers to capture enough cases, and a cross-sectional survey measures prevalence, not exposure preceding outcome.

items.stem: A small trial finds no difference in a rare outcome between two treatments, but only 20 patients were enrolled. The investigators conclude the treatments are equivalent. Which statistical concept best explains why this conclusion is unreliable?
options: A type I error is certain with small samples
Low power increases the chance of a type II error
A small sample always inflates the p value to 1
Confidence intervals cannot be computed for small trials
items.explanation: Power equals one minus beta and rises with larger samples, larger effects, and lower variability. A trial of 20 patients has low power, so failing to reject the null hypothesis may reflect a type II error, a false negative, rather than true equivalence. Small samples do not guarantee a type I error, and they do not force the p value to 1. Confidence intervals can be computed, though they will be wide.

items.stem: A couple in a fertility program signed written directives about embryo disposition. After they separate, one partner asks the clinic to discard the embryos while the other objects. What should guide the clinic?
options: The written directives the couple signed before treatment
The wishes of the partner who requests it
The clinic director's personal judgment
A new verbal agreement made today by phone
items.explanation: Embryo disposition is governed by the written directives the couple signed at the start of treatment, which is why those documents must be clear and revisited when circumstances change. Honoring one partner's later demand over the signed directive invites dispute, and the clinic director's personal view is not a basis for action. A verbal agreement by phone does not replace a signed document.

items.stem: A 16-year-old comes alone to clinic requesting testing for a sexually transmitted infection and says her parents must not know. She uses her mother's health insurance. Which step best protects her confidentiality?
options: Call her mother to explain that the visit was routine care
Send results to the parents because she is still a minor
Delay testing until a parent is able to attend the visit
Arrange a confidential way to reach her and review insurance billing
items.explanation: Many states let minors consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infection, and teenagers who fear disclosure may skip care entirely. The clinician should ask how she can be reached confidentially and remember that an insurance explanation of benefits can reveal a visit to the policyholder. Calling the mother, mailing results to parents, or requiring a parent to attend all breach her privacy and risk delayed care.

items.stem: An institution informs staff that it will not permit any physician to discuss or refer for a requested service. A patient is turned away without information. How is this best judged?
options: It is a protected form of conscientious objection
It is acceptable if the patient can search online
It imposes belief and is not protected
It is acceptable since the physician is not involved
items.explanation: Conscientious objection is an individual matter and does not permit an institution to impose belief on a patient or to withhold information. Objectors must provide accurate information and timely referral, and institutions should plan so that patients are never left without care. Leaving the patient to search alone, or shielding individual physicians, does not meet these duties.

items.stem: A 29-year-old G1 woman who speaks only Vietnamese is at 38 weeks and needs consent for induction of labor. Her husband speaks some English and offers to translate. Which is the best approach?
options: Let her husband translate since he is present and willing
Use a qualified medical interpreter
Ask a bilingual housekeeping employee on the unit to help
Use gestures and a translated form, then obtain her signature
items.explanation: Federal civil rights law requires meaningful language access, and the standard is a qualified medical interpreter in person, by video, or by telephone. Relatives introduce errors, may filter information, and inhibit candid answers about sensitive history. A bilingual employee without interpreter training has the same weaknesses. A signature on a translated form does not show that she understood the risks and alternatives, so it cannot replace a conversation.

items.stem: A resident notices that a senior colleague smells of drug use and made two dosing errors this week. The colleague denies a problem. What is the resident's duty?
options: Report through the proper channel
Ignore it, since the colleague denies any problem
Warn the colleague privately and take no further action
Post the concern on social media to raise awareness
items.explanation: A colleague who appears impaired by illness, fatigue, or substance use creates a duty to protect patients. The resident should not ignore the concern or rely on the colleague's denial, and should report through the proper institutional channel, which also directs the colleague to help. A private warning alone leaves patients at risk, and posting on social media violates confidentiality and professionalism.

items.stem: A 34-year-old G3P2 woman at 39 weeks with a persistent fetal heart rate abnormality declines recommended cesarean birth after a full discussion. She is alert and understands the risks. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Seek a court order to proceed with cesarean birth
Respect her refusal, document it, and keep offering care
Tell her that refusal could lead to child protective action
Proceed under implied consent once she is sedated
items.explanation: A pregnant woman with capacity may decline any intervention, including cesarean birth, even when the fetus may be harmed. The appropriate response explores her reasons, corrects misunderstanding, offers acceptable alternatives, documents the informed refusal, and continues the best care she accepts. Court orders against a competent patient are not justified, threats are coercive and damage trust, and implied consent applies only when a patient cannot decide in an emergency.

items.stem: A physician fears that a patient who refuses blood products may bleed. The patient has capacity and has signed an informed refusal. What should the physician do?
options: Honor it, offer alternatives, and continue care
Transfuse covertly if she begins to bleed
End the physician-patient relationship
Request a court order for transfusion
items.explanation: A competent patient may decline any intervention, and her refusal does not end the relationship. The physician explores the reasons, offers acceptable alternatives, documents the informed refusal, and continues the best care she accepts. Covert transfusion is deception and battery, ending the relationship abandons her, and court orders against a capable patient are not justified.

items.stem: A new drug lowers a laboratory marker associated with preeclampsia, but no trial has shown fewer seizures, stillbirths, or maternal deaths. How should the clinician regard this evidence?
options: As proof that the drug improves maternal survival
As equal to a randomized trial of mortality
As a surrogate outcome that may not predict patient-important benefit
As a reason to prescribe it to every patient
items.explanation: Surrogate outcomes, such as a change in a laboratory value, do not always predict a change in what matters to the patient, such as survival or function. Without demonstrated reductions in seizures or deaths, benefit remains unproven. The marker change is not proof of survival benefit, does not carry the weight of a randomized mortality trial, and does not justify universal prescribing.

items.stem: A new diagnostic test is evaluated first in a high-prevalence referral clinic, then in a low-prevalence screening clinic. Which measure will change, assuming the test itself is unchanged?
options: Sensitivity
Specificity
Positive likelihood ratio
Positive predictive value
items.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test and do not depend on prevalence, and likelihood ratios are built from them. Predictive values depend heavily on prevalence. When prevalence falls, the positive predictive value falls and the negative predictive value rises, so the same test performs differently in the screening clinic than in the referral clinic, even though nothing about the test has changed.

items.stem: A 52-year-old patient tells her gynecologist she wants to start dating him now that her care has ended last week after years of treatment. Which response is most consistent with professional ethics?
options: Accept, since her consent makes any relationship acceptable
Accept, after transferring her chart to a colleague
Decline, because the dependence of the former patient may persist
Decline only if she is still taking a prescribed medication
items.explanation: Sexual or romantic contact with a current patient is unethical regardless of consent. With a former patient, the judgment depends on how long ago care ended and on the likelihood that the earlier power imbalance and dependence remain. Care that ended only a week ago, after years of intimate treatment, falls clearly on the wrong side. Transferring the chart does not remove the imbalance, and the medication is irrelevant.

items.stem: A 48-year-old woman is scheduled for a hysterectomy at a teaching hospital. She asks whether residents will take part in her operation. What should the consent discussion include?
options: Nothing, since residents are always supervised
Only that the surgeon will be in the room
That residents participate only if she agrees afterward
That residents will participate under supervision
items.explanation: Residents work under supervision, and patients are entitled to know who performs which part of an operation. Consent for surgery should state that residents will participate. Omitting this, mentioning only the attending's presence, or asking for permission after the operation fails to respect her right to know in advance. Supervision matches the trainee's demonstrated skill, which the patient is also entitled to understand.

items.stem: A test is applied to 500 women who do not have the disease. It is positive in 50 of them. What is the specificity of the test?
options: 10 percent
90 percent
50 percent
95 percent
items.explanation: Specificity is the proportion of people without disease who test negative. Of 500 women without disease, 50 test positive and 450 test negative, so specificity is 450 divided by 500, or 90 percent. The figure 10 percent is the false positive rate, its complement. The figure 50 is merely the count of false positives. The figure 95 percent is not derivable from these numbers and is a distractor.

items.stem: A diagnostic test for a condition has a sensitivity of 80 percent and a specificity of 90 percent. What is the positive likelihood ratio?
items.explanation: The positive likelihood ratio equals sensitivity divided by one minus specificity, so 0.80 divided by 0.10 equals 8. A value well above 10 changes the probability of disease substantially, and 8 is moderately useful. The figure 0.22 is the negative likelihood ratio, 0.20 divided by 0.90. The figure 0.89 mixes the quantities incorrectly, and 72 arises from multiplying instead of dividing.

items.stem: After a wrong-dose medication error on the labor floor, a committee proposes three corrective actions. Which would be the strongest action according to the hierarchy of action strength?
options: A reeducation session for the nurses
A new written policy on dose checking
A forcing function that blocks the wrong dose
A reminder posted in the medication room
items.explanation: Action items are ranked by strength. Strong actions change the system, such as a forcing function or standardized equipment that makes the error impossible or very hard. Education, new policies, and reminders are weak actions because they depend on memory and vigilance. The goal of a root cause analysis is to find system causes and not culprits, so system redesign outranks efforts to change individual behavior.

items.stem: In a group of 200 women, 40 have a disease. A test is negative in 150 of the 160 women without disease and negative in 8 of the women with disease. What is the negative predictive value?
options: 94.9 percent
93.8 percent
80 percent
20 percent
items.explanation: Negative tests include 150 true negatives and 8 false negatives, for 158 in total. Negative predictive value is the proportion of negative tests that are true, 150 divided by 158, or 94.9 percent. The figure 93.8 percent is the specificity, 150 of 160. The figure 80 percent is the sensitivity, 32 of 40. The figure 20 percent is the false negative rate. Predictive values shift with prevalence, unlike those measures.

items.stem: After a hemorrhage event, a unit leader reports that three nurses will be retrained. A strong corrective action instead would include which change?
options: A memo reminding staff to be careful
A new policy that is only emailed
Retraining on the topic once a year
Standardized, pre-stocked hemorrhage kits
items.explanation: Action items are ranked by strength. Strong actions change the system, such as standardization and forcing functions, while education, memos, and policies that rely on memory are weak. Pre-stocked, standardized kits remove variation and make the right response easy. Reminders, an emailed policy, and annual retraining depend on individual vigilance and are likely to fail under stress.

items.stem: A 15-year-old at 12 weeks of gestation comes to prenatal care alone and asks that her parents not be told. Many jurisdictions allow minors to consent to pregnancy-related care. What is the physician's best approach?
options: Refuse care until a parent gives permission
Provide care, protect confidentiality, and explain the limits first
Inform her parents at the end of the visit
Refer her away because she is under 18 years old
items.explanation: Confidentiality extends to the adolescent's own visit, and many states let minors consent to pregnancy-related care. Teenagers who fear parental notice may avoid care, and delayed prenatal care causes greater harm. The physician should explain the limits, such as abuse or imminent risk of serious harm, before she discloses anything. Requiring parental permission, notifying parents, or referring her away would each deter care.

items.stem: A 29-year-old in active labor at 5 cm is handed a sterilization consent form by a resident, who says it must be signed now to have the tubal ligation tomorrow. What is the best response?
options: Defer consent until she is out of labor
Obtain the signature now to save time
Have her sign only if her partner agrees
Obtain verbal consent and fill in the form later
items.explanation: Sterilization consent safeguards were created to prevent coercion, and consent should not be obtained while the patient is in labor or seeking an abortion. Pain, stress, and urgency compromise voluntariness. The decision should be revisited when she can reflect, and an unsigned form must not delay urgent obstetric care. A partner's agreement is not required, and a form filled in after verbal consent would be invalid.

items.stem: A guideline panel reports that a service has moderate net benefit with high certainty of evidence. According to the United States Preventive Services Task Force system, which grade does this recommendation receive?
options: Grade C
Grade D
Grade B
Statement I
items.explanation: Grade A and grade B both recommend the service, grade A for substantial net benefit and grade B for moderate net benefit with adequate certainty. Grade C advises offering the service selectively, based on the individual patient. Grade D recommends against it because harm equals or outweighs benefit. The I statement means evidence is insufficient to judge the balance, which does not fit a finding of moderate benefit with high certainty.

items.stem: A 36-year-old with a high-risk pregnancy and a need for a cardiac specialist plus intensive care lives in a region with a Level II hospital and a Level IV center. Which plan is best?
options: Deliver at the Level II hospital and transfer if needed
Deliver at home with a midwife
Wait for labor to start before deciding
Plan delivery at the Level IV center
items.explanation: Levels of maternal care match risk to resources. Level IV is regional perinatal care with on-site medical and surgical subspecialists for the most complex patients, and transfer should happen before the emergency, whenever possible. Level II lacks the intensive and cardiac capability. Home birth and waiting until labor starts delay access to the care that her risk demands.

items.stem: A health department considers a screening program for a condition that has no accepted treatment and no recognizable latent stage. Which criterion for a worthwhile screening program is most clearly unmet?
options: A test that is safe and acceptable to patients
Treatment and a latent stage
A condition that is an important health problem
Systematic follow up for abnormal results
items.explanation: A worthwhile screening program requires a condition with a recognized latent stage and known natural history, a safe and acceptable test, an accepted treatment, and evidence that earlier treatment improves outcome. Without a treatment or a detectable preclinical phase, finding disease early can only add anxiety and cost. The condition may well be important, and the test may be safe, and follow up can be organized, so none of those is the clear deficiency.

items.stem: A 33-year-old with one prior low transverse cesarean birth is choosing between a trial of labor and repeat cesarean at 37 weeks. Both are reasonable. Which approach best reflects shared decision making?
options: Present balanced options and elicit her values
Recommend the option the physician prefers and obtain consent
Give her written materials and avoid discussion
Let her choose without describing the risks
items.explanation: Shared decision making is the model for preference-sensitive choices, such as mode of delivery after cesarean. The physician presents options in balanced terms, with benefits and harms in comparable formats, elicits the patient's values, and supports her in reaching a choice. A directive recommendation, materials without discussion, or a choice made without information each fail to engage her preferences or provide informed consent.

items.stem: A screening test reduces disease-specific mortality in randomized trials, and net benefit is judged substantial with high certainty. The recommending body issues which grade?
options: Grade B
Grade C
Grade D
Grade A
items.explanation: A grade A recommendation means that net benefit is substantial with high certainty, so the service should be offered. Grade B is for moderate net benefit with adequate certainty, grade C advises selective offering for small net benefit, and grade D recommends against a service when harm equals or exceeds benefit. Demonstrated mortality reduction in randomized trials is the strongest type of evidence for screening.

items.stem: A new patient is told that abortion law in her state changed last month. Her physician wants to counsel her accurately. What is the most appropriate principle to apply?
options: Memorize one fixed statute and apply it everywhere
Give evidence-based care within current local rules
Delay any care until counsel interprets the law
Withhold information to avoid legal risk
items.explanation: Abortion care is taught as a clinical service guided by principles: patient-centered, evidence-based, informed consent, confidentiality, and no judgment. Because state law varies and changes quickly, the physician must know current local rules but should rely on principles. Fixed memorization becomes wrong within a year, and delaying care or withholding information harms the patient without any legal requirement to do so.

items.stem: A 17-year-old requests a contraceptive implant. The clinician assumes she will not use condoms and suggests that an implant is best because of her age and background. Which is the best correction of this approach?
options: Insist on a barrier method alone for her age
Obtain parental permission before any counseling
Counsel without steering and honor her goals
Direct her toward the most effective method regardless of her goals
items.explanation: Adolescents deserve the same counseling about efficacy, risk, and alternatives as adults, and clinicians must not steer a patient toward a method based on assumptions about age, race, income, or disability. History of coerced sterilization shows why. Counseling should be directive about medical safety but not about the patient's goals. Parental permission is not generally required for contraception, and insisting on one method disregards her preferences.

items.stem: In a cohort study, preterm birth occurred in 24 of 200 women who had the exposure and in 8 of 200 women who did not. What is the relative risk of preterm birth with the exposure?
items.explanation: Risk in the exposed group is 24 of 200, or 12 percent, and risk in the unexposed group is 8 of 200, or 4 percent. Relative risk is the ratio of the two, 12 divided by 4, or 3. The figure 0.33 inverts the ratio. The figure 8 is the number of events in the unexposed group. The figure 16 is the difference in event counts, not a ratio of risks.

items.stem: A resident hears a laboring patient say she changed her mind about a planned epidural, but the family insists she proceed. The patient is alert. What is the best action?
options: Honor her current decision
Follow the family because they know her best
Proceed because she agreed earlier
Delay care until her wishes are reconfirmed in writing
items.explanation: A patient with capacity may withdraw consent at any time, and her present, voluntary choice governs. Family insistence does not override it, and an earlier agreement does not bind her. Voluntariness means freedom from pressure by clinicians or family, so requiring written reconfirmation would add a barrier rather than respect her choice, and would delay care she is entitled to decline.

items.stem: A new screening program detects many early lesions that, in follow-up studies, would never have caused symptoms or death. What term describes this problem?
options: Length bias
Lead-time bias
Recall bias
Overdiagnosis
items.explanation: Overdiagnosis is the extreme form of length bias, in which the detected lesion would never have mattered, and treating it brings harm without benefit. Length bias is the preferential detection of slow-growing disease. Lead-time bias lengthens measured survival by starting the clock sooner. Recall bias concerns memory of exposure in case-control studies and is unrelated to screen-detected lesions.

items.stem: A task force finds that a screening test for an asymptomatic condition causes substantial harm from false positives and overdiagnosis, with no mortality benefit. Which recommendation grade best fits this finding?
options: Grade A
Grade C
Grade D
Statement I
items.explanation: Grade D means the net benefit is zero or negative, so the service is recommended against. Here harm from false positives and overdiagnosis outweighs the absence of mortality benefit. Grade A recommends a service with substantial net benefit, grade C advises offering it to selected patients with small net benefit, and the I statement applies when evidence is too limited to judge, which is not the case when harm is established.

items.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 30 weeks develops sepsis from chorioamnionitis and is unstable in an emergency department. The staff states that a state law may limit what can be done. What is the best action?
options: Stabilize her at once, as federal law requires
Wait for hospital counsel to review the state law first
Transfer her first and stabilize at the receiving hospital
Obtain a second consultant opinion before any treatment
items.explanation: Federal law obliges hospitals with emergency departments to screen and stabilize anyone with an emergency medical condition, including a pregnant woman with sepsis. A physician must never delay emergency stabilization in the belief that law requires waiting. Legal review, an unstable transfer, and a second opinion all postpone treatment of a life-threatening condition that needs immediate care.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman arrives unconscious after a motor vehicle crash with brisk intraabdominal bleeding. No family is available. Surgery is needed within minutes. How should consent be handled?
options: Wait until a relative can be located to sign
Obtain a court order before the operation
Proceed under implied consent
Delay surgery until she regains consciousness
items.explanation: In a true emergency when delay threatens life or health and the patient cannot decide, treatment proceeds under implied consent, and the team explains what was done once she recovers. A reasonable patient would want lifesaving care. Searching for a relative, seeking a court order, or waiting for her to wake each adds a delay that could cost her life.

items.stem: A hospital plans to start a new process for blood transfusion consent and wants to predict where it might fail before launch. Which tool is most appropriate?
options: Root cause analysis
A surgical time-out
Severe morbidity review
Failure mode and effects analysis
items.explanation: Failure mode analysis is used before a process starts, to predict how it could fail and to prevent those failures. Root cause analysis is retrospective and follows a sentinel event. A time-out confirms patient, procedure, and site before incision. Severe morbidity review follows a qualifying case to find preventable factors. Only the prospective tool fits a process that has not yet begun.

items.stem: A recommendation in an obstetrics practice bulletin is based mainly on expert consensus and opinion, without randomized trials. Which evidence level does the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists assign?
options: Level A
Level C
Level B
Level D
items.explanation: Level A recommendations rest on good and consistent scientific evidence. Level B rests on limited or inconsistent evidence, and Level C rests on consensus and expert opinion. A recommendation without randomized trials, built on opinion, is Level C and should be held more loosely. A fourth letter is not part of the standard grading scheme, so that choice is not a real category.

items.stem: A labor and delivery unit wants to reduce deaths from postpartum hemorrhage. It stocks hemorrhage carts, runs drills, assesses risk on every admission, and debriefs each event. Which framework does this describe?
options: Failure mode and effects analysis of one process
A root cause analysis after a sentinel event
A just culture review of an individual clinician
A patient safety bundle for obstetric hemorrhage
items.explanation: Maternal safety bundles are organized around readiness, recognition and prevention, response, and reporting and systems learning. Stocked carts and drills are readiness, universal risk assessment is recognition, and event debriefing is reporting and learning. Failure mode analysis studies one process before it starts, root cause analysis follows a specific serious event, and a just culture review sorts individual behavior as error, at-risk, or reckless.

items.stem: A resident posts a photograph of an unusual ultrasound image on a personal social media account with the patient's name removed. The image includes a visible date, a rare diagnosis, and the hospital's name. What is the best assessment?
options: She could still be identified
It is acceptable because the name was removed
It is acceptable if her account is private
It is acceptable because it teaches
items.explanation: Patient information that could identify a person must not be posted, even without a name. A rare diagnosis, a date, and the hospital name together can identify the patient. Social media follows the same logic as every other form of communication. A private account, a removed name, or educational value does not change the obligation to protect confidentiality without the patient's permission.

items.stem: A labor nurse calls the on-call obstetrician about a patient with new severe-range blood pressures. Which structure best organizes this urgent communication?
options: I-PASS
A surgical time-out
SBAR
Root cause analysis
items.explanation: SBAR structures an urgent call to a senior colleague by stating the situation, the background, the assessment, and a recommendation. It speeds escalation and makes the request clear. I-PASS is a tool for handoff at transfer of care. A time-out confirms patient, procedure, and site before a procedure, and root cause analysis is a retrospective review after a serious event, so neither fits an urgent phone call.

items.stem: A 44-year-old woman with a terminal illness completed an advance directive naming her sister as agent. She now cannot speak, and her husband demands a different treatment than her written wishes. Who decides?
options: The husband, as the nearest relative
The sister, following the directive
The attending physician alone
The hospital administrator on call
items.explanation: An advance directive and a named health care agent express the patient's own choices while she had capacity. The agent decides according to her known wishes, and the written directive prevails over a relative's preference. A default order of relatives applies only when no directive or agent exists. The physician advises but does not replace the agent, and an administrator has no role in such a decision.

items.stem: A clinician repeatedly attributes a Black patient's severe headache and swelling in the postpartum period to anxiety. Which concept best describes this pattern, and what is a remedy?
options: Selection bias, addressed through randomization
Recall bias, addressed through chart review
Confounding, addressed through multivariable adjustment
Implicit bias, addressed by standard protocols
items.explanation: Implicit bias refers to automatic associations that shape judgment without conscious intent, such as discounting a patient's report of symptoms. It is addressed by naming it, using standardized protocols and early warning criteria, and listening carefully to the patient. Selection bias, recall bias, and confounding are research concepts with their own remedies and do not describe this clinical behavior.

items.stem: A drug reduces a stillbirth rate from 2 percent to 1 percent. A journalist reports that it halves stillbirth. How should the clinician explain the absolute benefit to a patient?
options: One fewer stillbirth per 100 treated women
Fifty fewer stillbirths per 100 treated women
The risk is cut by half for every patient
One fewer stillbirth per 10 treated women
items.explanation: A relative reduction of 50 percent corresponds to an absolute risk reduction of 1 percentage point, from 2 to 1 percent, so the number needed to treat is 100. A drug that halves a rare event may prevent very few events in absolute terms. Fifty fewer per 100 and one fewer per 10 greatly overstate the benefit, and halving is a relative statement.

items.stem: A review committee notes that Black women die of pregnancy-related causes at a rate several times higher than white women, even after adjusting for income and education. What is the best interpretation?
options: Individual behavior fully explains the difference
Structural factors contribute and most deaths are preventable
Genetic differences account for most of the gap
The gap disappears once insurance status is equal
items.explanation: The disparity persists across income and educational levels, so individual behavior does not explain it. Review committees conclude that most pregnancy-related deaths are preventable, and they point to unequal access, structural racism, differences in quality of care, and clinicians who discount reported symptoms. Genetics are not a supported explanation for the gap, and equalizing insurance alone does not remove it.

items.stem: A study finds that women who take a supplement have fewer miscarriages, but they also exercise more and smoke less. These factors are linked to both the supplement and miscarriage. What does this describe?
options: Effect modification, reported by subgroup
Recall bias, controlled by blinding
Confounding, controlled by randomization or adjustment
Type II error, controlled by larger samples
items.explanation: Confounding occurs when a third factor is associated with both exposure and outcome and is not on the causal pathway. It is controlled by randomization, restriction, matching, or multivariable adjustment. Effect modification differs in that the effect itself varies across strata. Recall bias arises from unequal memory of exposures, and type II error is a failure to detect a real difference.

items.stem: A hospital adopts a bundle for severe hypertension in pregnancy. Which element belongs to the response domain of the bundle?
options: Stocking antihypertensive supplies on the unit
A standard treatment pathway with timed treatment
Risk assessment of every patient at admission
Debriefing after each severe event
items.explanation: Bundles are organized around readiness, recognition and prevention, response, and reporting and systems learning. A standard treatment pathway with timely treatment is response. Stocked supplies and drills are readiness, universal assessment and early warning criteria are recognition, and debriefing and review of each event belong to reporting and systems learning. Each domain has a distinct purpose, so the answer depends on timing.

items.stem: A pregnant woman with a severe language barrier receives written discharge instructions in English at a high reading level. She returns with a complication she was told to watch for. What was the key failure?
options: No translated materials at a usable reading level
The patient failed to follow directions
The instructions were too short
A relative should have read them to her
items.explanation: Communication across language and literacy barriers is a safety and equity issue. Written materials should be offered in the patient's language and at a reading level that she can use. Blaming the patient ignores system responsibility, short instructions are not the problem here, and relatives are ad hoc interpreters whose use introduces error and inhibits candid disclosure of sensitive history.

items.stem: A multicenter trial compares two induction methods. Which feature best protects against confounding by both measured and unmeasured factors?
options: Matching on age only
Adjusting for parity only
Following patients for longer
Random assignment of the method
items.explanation: Randomization assigns exposure by chance, so measured and unmeasured confounders are balanced between groups on average. Matching on age or adjusting for parity addresses only the factors that were measured and chosen. Longer follow up affects the observed outcomes but does not change which patient characteristics differ between the groups, so confounding would remain unaddressed.

items.stem: A physician faces a conflict: a patient wants an intervention that the physician believes will not help but will not harm her. Which two ethical principles are most directly in tension?
options: Justice and nonmaleficence
Beneficence and nonmaleficence
Autonomy and beneficence
Autonomy and justice
items.explanation: Autonomy is the right of a capable patient to decide about her own body, while beneficence is the duty to act for her benefit. Here the patient's choice conflicts with the physician's view of what helps. Nonmaleficence is not at issue because the intervention is not expected to harm. Justice concerns fair distribution of resources and burdens, which is not the primary conflict in this scenario.

items.stem: An obstetrician with a moral objection to sterilization is asked for a postpartum tubal ligation by a stable patient with a valid consent. Which action best fits the duties of conscientious objection?
options: Decline to discuss the topic and tell her to look elsewhere for it
Perform the procedure while documenting disapproval
Delay the request until she reconsiders her decision
Give honest information and arrange a timely transfer of care
items.explanation: Conscientious objection is permissible when the physician gives accurate information and refers or transfers the patient promptly so that access is not delayed. Refusing even to discuss the topic withholds information and leaves the patient without a path to care. Performing the procedure under protest contradicts the physician's own conscience. Deliberate delay pressures the patient and imposes the physician's belief on her.

items.stem: A screening test is given to 400 women. Of 100 women with the disease, 80 test positive. Of 300 women without the disease, 270 test negative. What is the sensitivity of the test?
options: 90 percent
73 percent
80 percent
20 percent
items.explanation: Sensitivity is true positives divided by all people with disease: 80 of 100, or 80 percent. The figure 90 percent is the specificity, which is 270 of 300 women without disease. The figure 73 percent is the positive predictive value, 80 of 110 positive tests. The figure 20 percent is the false negative rate, the complement of sensitivity, and addresses a different question.

items.stem: A 26-year-old tells her resident that she is anxious and fears that her prenatal records will be seen by her employer. She asks who can access them. What is the best answer?
options: Those she authorizes and those caring for her
Anyone on the staff may view the chart
Her employer, as it pays for her insurance
Her relatives, if they call the clinic
items.explanation: Confidentiality is a core professional duty, and disclosure requires the patient's authorization, apart from narrow exceptions such as abuse, imminent serious harm, or statutory reporting. Staff access is limited to those who need it for her care. Neither an employer nor relatives who call the clinic may receive records without her explicit permission, so the clinician can reassure her accurately.

items.stem: A nurse administers a tenfold overdose after fatigue and a look-alike vial. The unit follows a just culture framework. How is this event classified, and how is it handled?
options: Reckless behavior, managed by discipline
Honest error, managed by fixing the system
At-risk behavior, managed by termination
Negligence, managed by legal reporting only
items.explanation: A just culture separates honest error, which is managed by consoling the person and fixing the system, from at-risk behavior, which is coached, and from reckless behavior, which is disciplined. A fatigued nurse and a look-alike vial reflect a system design problem. Discipline or termination would treat an honest error as reckless and would discourage reporting, and legal reporting alone does nothing to prevent recurrence.

items.stem: A 24-week pregnant woman with severe preeclampsia and a worsening neurologic examination presents to a Level I maternity hospital with no maternal-fetal medicine service or intensive care unit. Which is the best action?
options: Keep her at the Level I hospital and consult by telephone only
Discharge her with close outpatient blood pressure checks
Await progression to eclampsia before arranging transfer
Stabilize her and transfer her to a higher level of care
items.explanation: Levels of maternal care match the risk of a pregnancy to facility resources. Level III or IV centers provide maternal-fetal medicine, intensive care, and the capacity to manage complex disease. A patient this ill at a basic facility should be stabilized and transferred early, and the receiving center should accept her without delay. Telephone advice alone leaves the capability gap, discharge is unsafe, and waiting for an eclamptic seizure defeats the purpose of early transfer.

items.stem: In a cohort study, 30 of 100 smokers and 15 of 100 nonsmokers develop a pregnancy complication. What is the relative risk of the complication in smokers?
items.explanation: Relative risk is the risk in the exposed group divided by the risk in the unexposed group. Smokers have a risk of 30 percent and nonsmokers 15 percent, so the ratio is 0.30 divided by 0.15, or 2.0. The figure 0.5 inverts the ratio. The figure 15 is the absolute risk difference in percentage points, not a ratio. The figure 1.5 results from dividing 30 by 20, which has no basis in these data.

items.stem: A 22-year-old woman with a mild intellectual disability asks for contraception. Her guardian wants her sterilized. She can describe how pregnancy happens and why she wants a method. What is the best approach?
options: Presume capacity and counsel her directly
Defer entirely to the guardian's decision
Perform sterilization because it is simplest
Refuse contraception until she is older
items.explanation: A patient with an intellectual disability is presumed to have capacity for decisions she can understand, and she should receive the same counseling about efficacy, risk, and alternatives as anyone else. History of coerced sterilization of marginalized women led to current consent safeguards. Deferring wholly to a guardian, choosing permanent sterilization for convenience, or refusing contraception ignores her demonstrated understanding and goals.

items.stem: In a case-control study, 40 of 100 women with a birth defect and 20 of 100 control women reported a particular exposure. What is the odds ratio for the exposure?
items.explanation: Among cases, 40 were exposed and 60 were not, giving odds of 40 over 60. Among controls, 20 were exposed and 80 were not, giving odds of 20 over 80. The odds ratio is (40 times 80) divided by (60 times 20), or 3200 divided by 1200, which is about 2.7. The figure 2.0 is the ratio of proportions, a relative risk, which a case-control design cannot estimate. The figure 0.37 inverts the ratio.

items.stem: A new screening program reports that survival measured from the time of diagnosis has lengthened, yet deaths from the disease have not changed. Which bias best explains this finding?
options: Lead-time bias
Recall bias
Attrition bias
Effect modification
items.explanation: Earlier detection starts the survival clock sooner, so measured survival from diagnosis lengthens even when death occurs at the same time. This is lead-time bias. Recall bias affects case-control studies in which patients remember exposures differently, attrition bias arises when participants lost to follow up differ from those who stay, and effect modification means the true effect differs across strata. The remedy is to compare disease-specific mortality in a randomized trial.

items.stem: A woman with capacity agrees to a blood transfusion during a planned cesarean birth, but her chart contains only a signature on a preprinted form. What best describes valid informed consent?
options: The signature itself
A verbal agreement alone, with no record
A family member's approval on her behalf
A process of communication, then documentation
items.explanation: Informed consent is a process of communication and not a signature on a form. The physician discloses the diagnosis, treatment, material risks, benefits, and alternatives, the patient shows understanding in her own words, and the choice is voluntary. Documentation records that the conversation occurred and does not substitute for it. A capable patient decides for herself, so family approval is not a substitute.

items.stem: In a trial of a new drug to prevent preterm birth, the event rate was 10 percent in the control group and 6 percent in the treated group. What is the number needed to treat?
items.explanation: Absolute risk reduction is 10 percent minus 6 percent, or 4 percent, which is 0.04. The number needed to treat is its reciprocal, 1 divided by 0.04, or 25. The figure 4 is the absolute risk reduction expressed in percentage points, not its reciprocal. The figure 10 is the control event rate in percent. The figure 40 results from inverting a relative risk reduction of 40 percent, a different quantity.

items.stem: An ethics consultation is requested after a patient and her physician cannot agree on a plan despite repeated, respectful discussion. What is the primary role of the ethics consultant?
options: To overrule the patient's decision
To help clarify values and options, not to decide for the patient
To protect the hospital from liability
To select the plan that the physician prefers
items.explanation: Ethics consultation offers a structured analysis of the medical facts, patient preferences, quality of life, and contextual factors, and helps weigh autonomy, beneficence, nonmaleficence, and justice. It advises the team and patient and does not overrule a capable patient. Its purpose is not to limit liability for the institution, nor to rubber stamp the physician's preferred plan.

items.stem: During a vacuum delivery, a shoulder dystocia occurs and the infant sustains a brachial plexus injury. The mother asks what happened. What is the most appropriate response from the attending physician?
options: Wait for the risk management review before saying anything
Tell her the injury was unavoidable without further detail
Disclose, apologize, and describe the plan
Record the discussion in the chart as an incident report
items.explanation: When a patient is harmed, the physician discloses what happened promptly in plain language, accepts responsibility without speculating about blame, apologizes sincerely, and explains how the problem will be corrected. Waiting for institutional review delays honesty, and declaring the injury unavoidable offers false reassurance. The incident report belongs in the institution's safety system, never in the medical record, while the disclosure conversation is documented factually.

items.stem: Two guideline bodies give different recommended screening intervals for the same population. What is the most helpful way for a clinician to respond to this disagreement?
options: Follow the more frequent schedule in every patient
Ignore both and use personal preference
Assume the newer guideline must be correct
Review how each panel graded evidence and harm
items.explanation: Guidelines may differ because of different weighting of benefit and harm, evidence cutoffs, populations, or views of cost and access, so the disagreement is informative. A careful reader asks who wrote the guideline, how evidence was searched and graded, and whether conflicts were disclosed. Choosing the most intensive schedule, personal preference, or recency alone does not address the reason for the difference.

items.stem: A night-shift resident hands off six laboring patients to the day team in a hallway, summarizing each in one sentence. A missed pending culture later delays treatment. Which tool would best standardize this transfer of responsibility?
options: I-PASS, a structured handoff tool
SBAR, used once a patient deteriorates overnight
A root cause analysis done before any harm occurs
A surgical time-out repeated at each shift change
items.explanation: I-PASS is a handoff tool built to standardize transfer of care. It covers illness severity, a patient summary, an action list, situation awareness, and synthesis by the receiver, which would capture a pending culture. SBAR structures an urgent call for help, not routine transfers. Root cause analysis is retrospective and follows an event. A time-out confirms patient, procedure, and site before a procedure, not at shift change.

items.stem: A resident is asked by a supervisor to perform a pelvic examination on an anesthetized patient solely for teaching. The surgical consent did not mention it. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Proceed because the patient is already anesthetized
Decline until she has given prior consent
Proceed after the supervisor documents the educational value
Perform it quickly so that no extra anesthesia time is used
items.explanation: A pelvic examination performed under anesthesia for teaching alone is unethical without prior consent from the patient. Patients are entitled to know who performs which part of a procedure and what is done while they are anesthetized. Her unconsciousness, the supervisor's rationale, or brevity do not replace consent, and a trainee who is uneasy should raise the concern rather than comply.

items.stem: Women who volunteer for a screening program have lower mortality from many causes than women who decline, even from diseases unrelated to the test. Which bias does this describe?
options: Length bias
Lead-time bias
Recall bias
Healthy volunteer selection bias
items.explanation: People who choose screening tend to be healthier and to follow other preventive practices, so the screened group looks better regardless of the test. Lower mortality from unrelated causes is the clue. Length bias refers to slow-growing disease being detected preferentially. Lead-time bias lengthens measured survival by starting the clock sooner. Recall bias concerns differing memory of exposures in case-control studies. Randomized allocation is the remedy for these artifacts.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman, covered by public funds, signed a sterilization consent form 20 days ago and now requests the tubal ligation. She is not in labor. Why is the consent not yet valid?
options: At least 30 days must pass between signing and surgery
She must be at least 35 years old for the procedure
The signed form expires after only 10 days
Her spouse must also sign before surgery proceeds
items.explanation: When public funds pay for sterilization, federal rules require the patient to be at least 21 years old, to sign a specific form, and to wait at least 30 days after signing, with the consent no older than 180 days at surgery. Twenty days is too short. The age requirement is 21, not 35, and the form does not expire after 10 days. A spouse's signature is not required for an adult's own decision.

items.stem: A gynecologist is asked by a close friend to prescribe her a long-term hormone therapy and manage her chronic pelvic pain. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, since a friend will give an honest history
Accept and keep no record of the visits
Decline ongoing care and refer her to another physician
Prescribe only once and avoid examining her
items.explanation: Treating family members and close friends is discouraged except in emergencies, because objectivity and candid history suffer. An intimate relationship also blurs the boundaries of examination and confidentiality. Referral to another physician preserves both her care and the friendship. Keeping no record is unprofessional and unsafe for her, and a prescription without an examination is poor practice.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman is comatose after an amniotic fluid embolism and has no directive. Her husband says she often told him she would never want prolonged ventilator support. What standard guides his decision?
options: Best interests, set aside her stated views
Substituted judgment, based on her known wishes
The hospital ethics committee's own preference
The physician's estimate of her prognosis alone
items.explanation: When capacity is lacking and no directive exists, a surrogate decides according to the patient's known wishes, a standard called substituted judgment. Her repeated statements are exactly the kind of evidence it uses. The best interests standard applies only when her wishes are unknown. An ethics committee advises and does not replace the surrogate, and prognosis informs the choice but does not decide it.

items.stem: A patient brings her gynecologist an expensive piece of jewelry after a successful surgery and asks him to accept it. Which response is most consistent with professional standards?
options: Accept it and keep it private
Accept it and give her a discount on future care
Accept it only if it is wrapped
Decline graciously, since it creates obligation
items.explanation: Gifts of small value may be accepted graciously, while gifts that create obligation are declined, because the physician-patient relationship carries a power imbalance that the physician must manage. An expensive item can compromise objectivity or create a sense of debt. Accepting it quietly, trading it for favored treatment, or setting a wrapping condition does not remove that concern.

items.stem: A 30-year-old patient is counseled before a myomectomy. The surgeon omits a small risk of hysterectomy for uncontrolled bleeding. The patient has told the team that preserving her uterus matters above all. Why is the disclosure inadequate?
options: This patient would want to know that risk
Only common risks need to be disclosed
A signed form already covers every possible risk
Disclosure of rare outcomes causes needless anxiety
items.explanation: Disclosure is judged by what a reasonable patient would want to know, so a risk that is rare but catastrophic, or one that matters greatly to this particular woman, must be mentioned. Loss of the uterus is exactly that for her. A signed form records a conversation and does not replace it, and avoiding anxiety does not justify withholding a material risk.

items.stem: A gynecologic surgery team is about to begin a laparoscopic salpingectomy. The nurse notices that consent lists the left side, and the surgeon's draping suggests the right. Which safety step is designed to catch this error?
options: A root cause analysis after the operation
A surgical time-out confirming patient, procedure, and site before incision
An I-PASS handoff at the end of the case
A failure mode review at the next committee meeting
items.explanation: The surgical time-out occurs before incision. The team confirms the right patient, procedure, and site and states concerns aloud, and the culture must let any member stop the process without penalty. Root cause analysis and committee review happen after the fact, and a handoff at the end of the case cannot prevent a wrong-site operation that is about to occur.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with long-standing bipolar disorder, currently stable, declines a recommended hysterectomy for symptomatic fibroids. Her surgeon doubts her judgment because of the diagnosis. What is the best next step?
options: Obtain consent from her sister as surrogate
Treat the diagnosis as proof that capacity is absent
Assess her capacity for this specific decision
Proceed because the surgery is clearly in her interest
items.explanation: Capacity is the ability to make a particular decision at a particular time. It requires that she understand the information, appreciate how it applies to her, reason about the options, and express a stable choice. A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself remove capacity, and neither does a decision the surgeon considers unwise. A surrogate is appropriate only when capacity is actually lacking, and operating over a capable refusal violates autonomy.

items.stem: A case series of ten women with a rare tumor describes their clinical course without a comparison group. What is the most appropriate use of this evidence?
options: To generate hypotheses for stronger studies
To prove a treatment's effectiveness
To estimate incidence in the population
To calculate a relative risk
items.explanation: A case series describes patients without a comparison group and can generate hypotheses but cannot test them. It cannot establish effectiveness because there is no control. It cannot estimate incidence because the denominator is unknown, and relative risk requires comparison between exposed and unexposed groups. A randomized trial is the strongest design for testing a treatment.

items.stem: A clinician explains the benefit of mammography to a patient who prefers clear numbers. Which presentation is the most effective way to communicate the absolute benefit and harm?
options: A relative risk reduction alone
Natural frequencies for benefit and harm alike
Percentages for benefit and natural frequencies for harm
A statement that experts recommend screening
items.explanation: Absolute numbers communicate risk more clearly than relative ones, and natural frequencies such as three in 1,000 women are easier to grasp than percentages. Benefit and harm should be stated in the same format so the patient can compare them. A relative risk reduction alone can exaggerate small absolute effects, mixing formats hinders comparison, and an appeal to expert opinion does not support shared decision making.

items.stem: A hospital screens deliveries for severe maternal morbidity. Which finding on its own meets a widely used screening criterion for review?
options: Postpartum blood loss of 600 mL after cesarean birth
Treatment of mild hypertension at 37 weeks
A third-degree perineal laceration repaired in the labor room
Transfusion of four or more units of blood products
items.explanation: A widely used severe maternal morbidity screen is transfusion of four or more units of blood products or admission of the mother to an intensive care unit. Review aims to find preventable factors, and such cases are many times more common than deaths. Moderate blood loss, mild hypertension, and a repaired laceration do not meet the screening criteria, although each may receive its own quality attention.

items.stem: A screening test detects mostly slow-growing tumors with long preclinical phases, and cancers found by screening appear to carry a better survival than those found by symptoms. Which bias best explains the apparent advantage?
options: Recall bias
Observer bias
Length-time bias
Attrition bias
items.explanation: Length-time bias arises because screening preferentially finds slow-growing, indolent disease that persists long enough to be detected, so screen-detected cases look as if they live longer. Recall bias affects retrospective reports of exposure. Observer bias involves unequal measurement by assessors who know the exposure. Attrition bias comes from differential loss to follow up and does not depend on tumor growth rate.
